notes: Extradition oppression analysis is clear; judges metadata lists HHJ Mander but judgment is by Laws and Hallett.

enrichment.short_title: Austins: habeas corpus refused for Spanish escapee after cannabis sentence
key_facts: The applicant was sentenced in Spain in 1994 to over four years for cannabis possession after arrest on a Malaga-Barcelona train.
He absconded from a young offender institution in January 1995 and returned to the UK, acquiring a substantial criminal record including further drug and burglary offences.
Spanish extradition was requested but delayed until 2003 for formal proof he was unlawfully at large; he was committed on bail in April 2004.
He argued section 11(3)(b) made return oppressive because of Spanish delay, known whereabouts, and recent rehabilitation with a stable partner.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for writ of habeas corpus under section 11(3)(b) of the Extradition Act 1989 against committal to await the Secretary of State's extradition decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; oppression not shown and the applicant must await extradition to serve the balance of his lawful Spanish sentence.
enrichment.ratio: Section 11(3)(b) asks whether return would be oppressive by passage of time, not whether the requesting state acted dilatorily; where the fugitive escaped after trial and could not have been removed for most of the period because of section 12(3) and his own UK imprisonment, delay and recent settlement do not establish oppression.
legal_issues: Whether Spanish delay in seeking extradition made return oppressive
Application of section 12(3) where the fugitive was serving UK sentences
Whether the applicant was misled in 1996 that Spain did not want him
Distinction between injustice at trial and oppression on return to serve sentence

notes: Special reasons drink-driving appeal dismissed on clear facts; judges metadata incorrectly lists Lord Widgery.

enrichment.short_title: Khan: no special reasons to avoid disqualification after fatal accident scare
key_facts: Mr Khan drove about one mile on the A12 at about 4.40 am on New Year's Day 2004 after champagne on New Year's Eve.
He feared his teenage sons were involved in a nearby fatal road accident and drove through a police cordon to check; blood alcohol was nearly 2.5 times the limit at 6.20 am.
His wife, who had not drunk and had driven earlier, was asleep upstairs; magistrates found he could have woken her or walked in under 20 minutes.
Magistrates refused special reasons and disqualified him for three years; he appealed by case stated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' refusal to find special reasons not to disqualify for drink-driving.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; magistrates could reasonably find no special reasons and a sober reasonable friend would have advised not to drive.
enrichment.ratio: Special reasons for not disqualifying require clear compelling emergency objectively assessed; very high alcohol level, availability of a sober driver, and a short walkable distance weigh against discretion even where a father's fear for his children is understandable.
legal_issues: Whether perceived emergency on hearing of a fatal accident constituted special reasons
Objective test of sober reasonable and responsible friend under DPP v Bristow
Whether failure to wake a sober spouse was a reasonable alternative
Application of Taylor v Rajan guidance on high blood alcohol readings

confidence.notes: Facts, authorities and dismissal are explicit in Davis J's judgment.

notes: Care proceedings Human Rights Act damages appeal; Court of Appeal restored principled limits on Article 6 awards.

enrichment.short_title: Re V: care order appeal quashes nominal Article 6 damages for pre-birth social work
key_facts: Parents with three prior children removed and freed for adoption faced care proceedings for fourth child M born July 2003.
County court judge granted care and freeing orders but awarded each parent £100 nominal damages for pre-birth breach of Article 6 by inadequate social worker communication.
Parents had not clearly sought damages until late written submissions; local authority had missed meetings but parents withdrew section 38(6) assessment application at trial.
Neither parent attended the Court of Appeal hearing though notified.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Local authority appeal from county court care and freeing orders with nominal Human Rights Act damages for alleged Article 6 breach.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; nominal damages order set aside; pre-birth social work failures could not amount to Article 6 breach or justify damages under section 8.
enrichment.ratio: Article 6 fairness must be assessed viewing proceedings as a whole; isolating pre-birth social worker omissions before proceedings began cannot establish unfairness, and section 8 requires just satisfaction necessity before any damages award in care cases.
legal_issues: Whether pre-birth social work failures breached Article 6 ECHR
Misuse of paragraph 154 of Re L as mandatory good practice creating liability
Whether section 8 permitted nominal damages without just satisfaction analysis
Weeding out barren Human Rights Act arguments in care proceedings

Re V (Care Proceedings: Human Rights Claims) [2004] EWCA Civ 54

notes: Undue influence trust deed trial fully reasoned; judges metadata lists historical Law Lords not sitting.

enrichment.short_title: Humphreys v son: trust deed set aside but 60/40 beneficial shares ordered
key_facts: Elderly Mrs Humphreys bought her council house in 1989 with a 60% right-to-buy discount; son Dennis funded the mortgage and a trust deed gave him sale proceeds and joint consent powers.
Nearly 13 years later she sought to set aside the deed for undue influence, unconscionable bargain, misrepresentation or mistake.
Dennis paid mortgage instalments until 1994, resumed when able, and maintained the house; the property was worth about £180,000.
Judge found Dennis exercised undue influence as her trusted adviser but rejected other vitiating factors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial of claim to set aside 1989 trust deed and determine beneficial interests in the family home.
enrichment.outcome: Trust deed set aside for undue influence; constructive trust declared with 60% to Mrs Humphreys and 40% to Dennis reflecting discount and mortgage contributions; sale ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where a son assumed parental advisory role in a right-to-buy purchase and procured a trust deed transferring economic benefit to himself, undue influence may vitiate the deed; absent the deed, fair shares follow whole-course-of-dealing analysis treating the tenant's discount as her contribution to a £64,500 value purchase.
legal_issues: Whether Dennis's influence was undue in procuring the trust deed
Whether the deed was an unconscionable bargain or induced by misrepresentation
Common mistake as to parties' oral agreement on ownership
Quantification of beneficial interests after setting aside the deed
linked_authorities: Mumford v Ashe and others (2001) 33 HLR 756

confidence.notes: Findings and 60/40 quantification are explicit though judgment is lengthy and metadata is unreliable.

notes: ASBO appeal dismissed; exceptional need for geographical restraint after persistent offending.

enrichment.short_title: Parkinson: two-year ASBO upheld alongside YOI sentence for chain robbery
key_facts: Scott Parkinson robbed a DJ's neck chain in Preston in March 2004 after aggressive abuse; the chain was recovered from a female companion's clothing.
He received three years' detention in a YOI, rightly not challenged, plus a two-year ASBO from release.
He had 28 prior offences since 1999 including burglary, ABH and vehicle crime; Brookfield residents had suffered years of family antisocial conduct culminating in eviction.
Sentencing judge had detailed police and council evidence of persistent offending in hours of darkness in groups under alcohol.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal against anti-social behaviour order imposed with custodial sentence for robbery.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; ASBO was necessary and properly imposed as an exceptional case supplementing licence conditions.
enrichment.ratio: Following R v P, ASBOs are rarely appropriate where long custodial sentences and licence apply, but geographical restraints may still be necessary where formidable criminal history and community evidence show demonstrable need to protect the public beyond licence conditions.
legal_issues: Whether ASBO should follow substantial YOI sentence under R v P
Necessity of geographical restraint supplementing licence
Whether sentencing material on ASBO appeals must be before the Court of Appeal

confidence.notes: ASBO reasoning and dismissal are clearly stated by Royce J.

notes: Article 14 parole referral appeal succeeds on ambit point; judges metadata polluted with historical names.

enrichment.short_title: Hindawi and Headley: deportable prisoners need not be referred to Parole Board
key_facts: Hindawi serving 45 years for El Al bomb plot and Headley serving seven years for drug importation sought Parole Board referral before early release.
Deportation orders required their removal at sentence end; Secretary of State refused section 32(2) referral unlike prisoners not liable to removal.
McCombe J quashed refusals holding Article 14 required equal Parole Board involvement.
Carlisle Committee 1988 had recommended separate early-release regime for deportable prisoners.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State appeal from judicial review quashing refusal to refer deportable long-term prisoners to the Parole Board under section 32(2).
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; Article 14 not engaged because early release applications fall outside Article 5 ambit; Hindawi decision letter reasons adequate.
enrichment.ratio: Lawful detention under a determinate sentence satisfies Article 5 for its term so Article 14 cannot secure non-discriminatory parole procedures; Parliament's Carlisle-based distinction excluding deportable prisoners from mandatory Parole Board referral is objectively justified.
legal_issues: Whether Article 5 ambit covers applications for early release on licence
Article 14 discrimination between deportable and non-deportable long-term prisoners
Justification of Carlisle Committee separate regime under section 46
Adequacy of Hindawi early release refusal letter
linked_authorities: R (Clift) v Secretary of State [2004] EWCA Civ 514
South Bucks DC v Porter [2004] 1 WLR 1953

confidence.notes: Majority outcome on Article 14 is clear though judgments are long and divided on reasoning.

notes: Speed limit judicial review; sentence quashed not conviction under section 142 remittal.

enrichment.short_title: Harrison: excessive speeding penalty quashed; remittal under section 142
key_facts: Claimant drove at 67 mph on B5441 Welsh Road where national speed limit applied not 30 mph limit police believed.
She pleaded guilty to exceeding 30 mph limit and received £130 fine, six points and 42-day disqualification.
Police discovered error in October 2002 and wrote to affected motorists but she had already pleaded; solicitors delayed judicial review over 14 months.
She would likely have faced only three points under ACPO guidelines for 60 mph limit road.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Late judicial review of magistrates' conviction and sentence for speeding on wrong speed limit.
enrichment.outcome: Sentence quashed and remitted to magistrates to reopen under section 142(1); conviction not set aside as offence under section 89 was committed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a motorist was guilty of exceeding a speed limit under section 89 but sentenced on mistaken 30 mph limit facts, quashing the sentence and remitting for section 142 rectification is the just remedy rather than vacating a lawful conviction.
legal_issues: Whether conviction should be quashed when wrong limit was charged
Relief despite 14-month delay in bringing judicial review
Use of section 142 to replace excessive disqualification and points
Whether ACPO guidelines affect sentencing on remittal

confidence.notes: Remittal remedy and reasoning on conviction versus sentence are explicit.

notes: Barecon owner-option arbitration clause; Morison J granted section 9 stay.

enrichment.short_title: NB Three v Harebell: owner may stay charterparty claim under one-sided arbitration option
key_facts: Charterers sued owners over interest rate certification and alleged overcharging on two Barecon 89 bareboat charters for Arctic Trader and Arctic Voyager.
Clause 47 gave owners option to refer disputes to arbitration while charterers could only sue in English courts.
Owners issued court proceedings then exercised arbitration option and sought stay under section 9; charterers sought mandatory disclosure orders.
Dispute included termination events, interest certificates and alleged secret profit on financed vessel purchases.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court applications for stay under section 9 of the Arbitration Act 1996 and for section 44 interim disclosure.
enrichment.outcome: Stay granted under section 9; charterers' disclosure applications dismissed; disputes to be arbitrated in London at owners' option.
enrichment.ratio: A one-sided owner option in clause 47.02 to bring disputes to arbitration creates a binding arbitration agreement once exercised, and section 9 applies even where charterers properly commenced English proceedings first; disclosure is for the tribunal.
legal_issues: Construction of owner-only arbitration option in clause 47.02 Barecon 89
Whether section 9 applies after charterers properly brought court proceedings
Validity of non-mutual arbitration agreements under English law
Whether court should order pre-arbitration disclosure under section 44
linked_authorities: Lobb Partnership Ltd v Aintree Racecourse Co Ltd [2000] 1 BLR 65

notes: Confiscation orders reduced after judge's section 5 muddle; separate Hussain convictions refused.

enrichment.short_title: Hussain, Joyce and Marshall: confiscation orders reduced to realisable assets
key_facts: Three defendants convicted of May 2001 cocaine conspiracy; Marshall leader sentenced to 11 years, Hussain and Joyce to eight years.
Confiscation orders made in August 2002 for benefit figures of £2.52m, £400,000 and £235,000 though judge also stated lower realisable asset figures.
Judge adopted pragmatic focus on realisable assets but ultimately ordered full benefit amounts after rejecting defendants' evidence as lies.
Court of Appeal found section 5(3) test muddled and substituted orders at identified realisable amounts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeals against Drug Trafficking Act 1994 confiscation orders; Hussain also renewed sentence and later possession appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Confiscation orders quashed and replaced with realisable sums: Hussain £63,447, Joyce £70,116, Marshall £135,392; Hussain's other appeals refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 5(3) the defendant must satisfy the court realisable assets are less than total benefit; where the judge stated realisable figures in judgment but ordered full benefit without clear section 5 reasoning on hidden assets, confiscation must reflect known realisable property.
legal_issues: Application of section 5(3) burden on defendants to prove lower realisable amount
Whether rejection of defence evidence compels full benefit orders
Marshall property valuation as realisable asset versus cash lodgements only
Safety of Hussain's fingerprint possession conviction and consecutive sentence
linked_authorities: R v Ilsemann (1990) 12 Cr App R(S) 398

notes: R v G overturns Caldwell direction; substituted simple arson verdict with modest sentence reduction.

enrichment.short_title: Castle: Caldwell recklessness direction quashed; substituted arson intent verdict
key_facts: Castle burgled accountants' offices in St Albans and set fire using accelerant to destroy evidence; offices damaged about £150,000, flats above smoke damaged, occupants away.
Blood traces linked him to burglary; jury convicted arson reckless as to endangering life under Caldwell direction.
He received concurrent 18 months for burglary and four years for arson; House of Lords in R v G redefined recklessness subjectively.
Flats above were residential though unoccupied at midnight when fire lasted about 20 minutes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal against conviction for arson endangering life after guilty plea to burglary.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction quashed; substituted guilty verdict for simple arson with intent to damage; arson sentence reduced from four years to three and a half years concurrent.
enrichment.ratio: Following R v G, Caldwell objective recklessness directions cannot sustain convictions under section 1 Criminal Damage Act 1971; where jury must have been sure of intentional damage, section 3 substitution of simple arson verdict is appropriate.
legal_issues: Effect of R v G on Caldwell recklessness directions
Whether to order retrial or substitute section 3 verdict
Appropriate sentence for intentional arson to destroy burglary evidence
Distinction between simple arson and endangering life aggravated offence
linked_authorities: R v G and another [2004] AC 1034
